slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: First, let’s revisit the major scale
The diatonic, stepwise pattern of major and minor seconds creates the major scale, no matter the starting pitch

bullets: Now, let’s look at the diatonic collection as a circle

slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: In order to form a triad, we simply choose three non-adjacent pitch classes

diagrams.purpose: Circle of seconds highlighting C, E, G in red to show they are non-adjacent.

notation.purpose: C major scale in treble clef with notes C4, E4, and G4 highlighted (circled in red).
notation.derivationNote: C major scale (C4 to C5) in treble clef. The triad members C4, E4, and G4 are circled in red on the slide, modeled here with a 'highlighted' boolean property.

slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: A triad can be built on any scale degree, as long as we choose every other pitch class

diagrams.purpose: Circle of seconds highlighting C, E, G in red.
Circle of seconds highlighting E, G, B in red to show another triad built from E.

slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: Remember, because we are choosing three pitch classes from a seven-note collection, they will NOT be evenly spaced
Consider every triad as a collection of three non-adjacent solfege syllables
In this example, there is a larger space between Mi and La (P4) than between the other triad members, which are separated by thirds
This asymmetry will later help us to find the chordal root!

diagrams.purpose: Circle of seconds labeled with solfege syllables (Do at 12 o'clock), with Do, Mi, La highlighted in red to show the asymmetric spacing (large gap between Mi and La).

slides.title: NOT A TRIAD!
bullets: The following are examples of sonorities that are NOT triads!
Triads cannot have adjacent pitch classes, no matter how they are voiced

diagrams.purpose: Non-triad example highlighting adjacent notes C, E, B on the circle of seconds.
Non-triad example highlighting adjacent notes C, D, B on the circle of seconds.

slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: The quality of a triad is determined by the size/quality of the intervals between the voices
Begin by removing the pitches that lie in between the triad members
The root (which we will consider the “lowest” pitch) will be the furthest pitch counter-clockwise before the large gap of a fourth

diagrams.purpose: Circle of seconds with non-triad tones (D, F, A, B) hidden, leaving only C, E, G to show the asymmetric spacing clearly.

notation.purpose: Stacked C major triad on treble staff showing Major Third (lower third), minor third (upper third), and Perfect Fifth (bounding fifth).
notation.derivationNote: C major triad (C4-E4-G4) stacked vertically. The slide indicates the intervals: lower Major Third (M3), upper minor third (m3), and bounding Perfect Fifth (P5).

slides.title: THE CIRCLE OF THIRDS WHEEL
bullets: The letters always run in the same order around the wheel: C-E-G-B-D-F-A (and back to C)
To name a chord, read clockwise from its root: the next stop is the third, the one after that is the fifth, and a seventh chord adds one more
The root is the furthest pitch counter-clockwise before the large gap of a fourth — that gap is what tells you the chord has ended

diagrams.purpose: Circle of thirds wheel rooted on C, highlighting the C-E-G triad (root, third, fifth).
Circle of thirds wheel rooted on G, highlighting the G-B-D-F seventh chord (root, third, fifth, seventh).

slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: Each pitch in the triad bears a specific name
When stacked in a series of thirds, the lowest note is the root, the middle note is the third, and the top note is the fifth

notation.purpose: C major triad in treble clef with labels Root, Third, and Fifth pointing to each chord member.
notation.derivationNote: C major triad (C4-E4-G4) stacked. Note labels point to each notehead: Root on C4, Third on E4, Fifth on G4.

slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: There are four qualities of triads, based on the intervals between the chord members

tables.purpose: Triad quality definition table containing interval formulas and examples built on A.

notation.purpose: The four triad qualities built from A: diminished (A-C-Eb), minor (A-C-E), major (A-C#-E), and augmented (A-C#-E#).
notation.derivationNote: Diminished (A-C-Eb), minor (A-C-E), major (A-C#-E), and augmented (A-C#-E#) triads in treble clef. Qualities are derived from tertian stack formulas from A.

slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: What is the quality?  Stack the triad from root-third-fifth.
ID the bounding fifth
ID the lower third
If the bounding fifth is perfect, the triad will be either major or minor, depending on the quality of the lower third
If the bounding fifth is diminished, the triad will be diminished
If the bounding fifth is augmented, the triad will be augmented

notation.derivationNote: G minor triad (G4-Bb4-D5) in treble clef. The slide highlights the intervals: Minor Third (G to Bb) and Perfect Fifth (G to D).

slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: When describing the quality of a triad, we do so by naming the root and the quality
g minor

slides.title: DEFINING THE TRIAD
bullets: In jazz and popular music, we use a shorthand to describe triad quality
Root name and quality
G Major = G
g minor = G-, G min (or g min)
G Augmented = G+ (or G #5)
g diminished = G dim, Go (or g min b5)
the root named in the chord is also the note played by the bass

notation.purpose: G triads in jazz shorthand: G (G4-B4-D5), GMIN (G4-Bb4-D5), G+ (G4-B4-D#5), GDIM (G4-Bb4-Db5).
notation.derivationNote: Four chords on G demonstrating lead sheet labels. G major (G), G minor (GMIN) with Bb, G augmented (G+) with D# (courtesy natural on B), and G diminished (GDIM) with Bb and Db.

slides.title: Triads and figured bass
bullets: Figured bass (or Thoroughbass) refers to a shorthand system to designate the intervals to be played above the bass.
We will usually assume a four part texture when reading figured bass (Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass)
Since the intervals above the bass in a triad are a 3rd, a 5th, and an 8va, the full figure for a triad is 8/5/3

notation.purpose: Seven root-position triads in a four-part texture, each showing intervals 8/5/3 from the bass note.
notation.derivationNote: Four-part root-position chords over a given bass line. Chords are transcribed directly from the staves: C major, F major, G major, a minor, b diminished, C major (high), G major (low). Each chord is labeled with its full 8/5/3 figure.

slides.title: Triads and figured bass
bullets: Notice that the intervals in figured bass are the generic intervals from the bass. The note above the bass comes from the key unless indicated otherwise
Any alterations of the intervals from the bass will be indicated next to the numbers. Here are the general rules for alterations:
Any accidental next to a number indicates adding that accidental to that generic interval above the bass
A number with a + (or strikethrough) should be raised
A number with a - should be lowered

notation.purpose: Seven chords in G major illustrating figures and alterations (e.g. #3, 5/3).
notation.derivationNote: Key signature of G major (1 sharp). Chords are: e minor, C major, A major (with C# accidental, figure 8/5/#3), G major (3 voices, figure 5/3), a minor, B major (with D# accidental, figure 8/5/#3), e minor. Transcribed verbatim from the slide's staves.

slides.subtitle: Shorthand for triads
bullets: 8/5/3 triads are indicated by NO numbers in shorthand figured bass
This means that any bass note without figures is assumed to be an 8/5/3 triad
For example, in the following figured bass, every chord should be an 8/5/3
